meta.title: Who really said "From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Napoleon really did say it, twice, retreating from Russia. He did not invent it — the saying was in French print by 1777, decades before.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step'?
meta.ogDescription: Napoleon really did say it, retreating from Russia. He did not invent it — the saying was in French print by 1777, decades earlier.

answer.label: Said by Napoleon — but not coined by him
answer.sourceLine: He said it, and we can watch him say it. His ambassador to Warsaw, the Abbé de Pradt, published an account of their audience of 10 December 1812 ↗ in which Napoleon — fresh from the catastrophe in Russia — drops the line twice in one conversation. What he was not doing was inventing it: Quote Investigator ↗ finds the same sentence in French print in 1777, thirty-five years earlier, and concludes that the saying is best treated as anonymous.

source.heading: The audience at Warsaw

docMeta.dd: Histoire de l'ambassade dans le grand-duché de Varsovie en 1812
Dominique Dufour de Pradt, then French ambassador to Warsaw
10 December 1812, during the retreat from Russia

source.excerpt: Dangers! pas le moindre. Je vis dans l’agitation; plus je tracasse, mieux je vaux. Il n’y a que les rois fainéans qui engraissent dans les palais: moi, c’est à cheval et dans les camps. Du sublime au ridicule il n’y a qu’un pas.
trail: We read the primary. The full text of the 1815 edition ↗ contains “Du sublime au ridicule il n’y a qu’un pas” twice within de Pradt’s account of the same audience — consistent with his own remark that Napoleon repeated it. Two further independent scans of the 1815 printing give the same passage.
Wikiquote ↗ dates the remark to 10 December 1812 and attributes the record of it to de Pradt, citing Sir Archibald Alison’s History of Europe (1842), Vol. 3, p. 593 for the English rendering.

Quote Investigator ↗ is the reason this page says “not coined by him”. Its survey traces the saying back through Marmontel (1787), Joseph Warton (1782) and a 1777 collection, Pensées Nouvelles et Philosophiques, which prints “Du sublime au ridicule, disait Fontenelle, il n’y a qu’un pas”. QI notes that attribution is itself weak, since Fontenelle died in 1757, and concludes that an anonymous attribution is appropriate.
source.excerptNote: De Pradt’s French, as printed in 1815. Roughly: “Danger? Not the least. I live on agitation; the more I stir things up, the better I am. Only do-nothing kings grow fat in palaces — for me it is horseback and camps. From the sublime to the ridiculous is but a step.” The same sentence appears a second time a few pages earlier in the same audience.

author.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
author.heading: About Napoleon Bonaparte
author.bio: Napoleon Bonaparte rose through the artillery of the French Revolutionary army to crown himself Emperor of the French in 1804, and for a decade redrew the map of Europe. The invasion of Russia in 1812 destroyed his army and began the collapse that ended at Waterloo and, finally, in exile on Saint Helena. He was a compulsive talker, and a great deal of what we have from him survives because someone in the room wrote it down.

misattribution.heading: Who actually coined it
misattribution.intro: Napoleon is not being falsely credited with saying this — he said it. He is falsely credited with originating it.

items.why: The line is genuinely his to speak — de Pradt records it twice ↗ in December 1812. But it was already circulating in French thirty-five years before, so crediting him with the thought is a step too far.

A 1777 collection prints the sentence and credits Fontenelle. Quote Investigator ↗ treats this as the earliest close match it could find, while cautioning that the evidence is weak: Fontenelle had been dead twenty years when the book appeared.

Paine wrote a related but distinct formulation in The Age of Reason — “One step above the sublime, makes the ridiculous; and one step above the ridiculous, makes the sublime again” — which QI dates to 1795/96 ↗. It is a cousin of the saying, not this sentence.

misattribution.truthLine: Quote Investigator’s conclusion ↗ is that no originator can be established and “an anonymous attribution is appropriate”. Napoleon is the reason you have heard it.

context.heading: Why he said it then
lead: On 5 December 1812 Napoleon abandoned what was left of the Grande Armée in Russia and set off for Paris by sleigh. Five days later he turned up in Warsaw, unrecognised, at a hotel, and summoned his ambassador. De Pradt’s account is of a man talking without pause — boasting, deflecting, insisting he was in no danger — and returning again and again to the same sentence about the sublime and the ridiculous.

It reads less like an epigram than a tic: the most catastrophic reversal of his career, being talked down to the size of a witticism in real time. He had roughly half a million men when he crossed into Russia; he was now a passenger in a sleigh.
context.detailsSummary: What de Pradt actually wrote down
detailsBody: De Pradt was no neutral witness — Napoleon dismissed him after the Russian campaign and the memoir is, in part, his answer. That is worth knowing when reading it. What it does supply is a contemporaneous, published record by a man in the room, printed within three years of the conversation.
His own phrasing gives the game away on the coinage: he describes Napoleon “having repeated again two or three times” the line. It was a saying being reached for, not one being made.

Quote Investigator traces the saying to a 1777 French collection crediting Fontenelle (d. 1757), documents Paine’s 1795/96 related formulation and de Pradt’s 1815 record, and concludes an anonymous attribution is appropriate.
Wikiquote dates the remark to 10 December 1812, attributes the record to Abbé de Pradt, and cites Alison’s History of Europe Vol. 3 (1842), p. 593.
The Internet Archive holds a full-view scan of de Pradt's Histoire de l'ambassade dans le grand-duché de Varsovie en 1812, published 1815.
